keyVerseText: And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly; and the dirt came out. the dirt: or, it came out at the buttocks
rootMeaning: The root of פַּרְשְׁדֹן (parshᵉdôn) is connected to the Hebrew root פָּרָשׁ (pârâsh), which means to scatter, separate, or make distinct. The etymology suggests a compound involving the idea of straddling or separation, possibly referencing a physical or spatial division. This root sense of separation or distinction adds a vivid literal dimension to the word beyond the English gloss of "dirt" or "excrement," implying something that is set apart or expelled from the body.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Judges 3:22, where it is translated as "and the dirt" or understood as something coming out at the buttocks. The limited occurrence and its translation highlight its reference to physical waste or excrement, which is a rare and strikingly concrete term in the biblical text. The consistency in translation as "dirt" or excrement reveals its primary association with unclean, rejected matter expelled from the body.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פַּרְשְׁדֹן in its original Hebrew context underscores the biblical attention to the physical realities of human life, including those aspects often seen as unclean or dishonorable. The presence of such a term in Scripture reminds believers of the fallen, broken nature of humanity and the bodily frailty that sin has brought into the world. Yet, it also points to God's sovereignty over all aspects of life, even those that seem shameful or repulsive. In Christ, the ultimate cleansing and restoration of both body and soul is accomplished, transforming what was once rejected into a testimony of grace.
keyVerseReflection: In Judges 3:22, the phrase describing the "dirt" coming out as the dagger is stuck in the enemy's belly vividly portrays the fatal injury and the physical consequences of the act. The use of פַּרְשְׁדֹן here emphasizes the totality of the wound—so severe that even what is normally hidden and unclean is expelled. This detail deepens the imagery of defeat and judgment, illustrating the thoroughness of God's deliverance through the hand of His servant.
